result.summary: Pausanias argues that elephant tusks are horns, not teeth, citing animals and his own sight of a skull in Campania. He then describes offerings in the temple of Zeus at Olympia: Antiochus' veil, Arimnestus' throne, Cynisca's horses, imperial statues and Nero's gifts.

scenes.title: Are elephant tusks horns?
scenes.summary: Pausanias argues from other animals and from fire-shaping that tusks are horns. He cites a skull seen near Capua and notes Greek use of ivory.

scenes.title: Offerings in the temple at Olympia
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists votive gifts in the temple of Zeus: the veil of Antiochus, Arimnestus' throne, Cynisca's horses, emperors' statues and Nero's offerings. He digresses on Trajan, Nicomedes and amber.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias insists on personal observation rather than hearsay.

analysis.text: Pausanias combines reasoned natural inquiry with a catalogue of sacred dedications, showing his interest in both evidence and piety.
The Roman emperors' statues at Olympia show how Greek sanctuaries honoured imperial power in the second century AD.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias is right that tusks are not horns, but his observations of their growth show ancient comparative reasoning.

language_notes.text: "Celtic elks" refers to elk-like deer of Celtic lands (northern Europe); the exact animal is uncertain. Pausanias uses it as an example of unusual horns.
"Antelopes" translates a Greek word for horned animals; the precise species is uncertain, but the point is that horns regrow or are replaced.
"Acted upon by fire" means heated and softened; Pausanias claims horn can be straightened or reshaped by heat, while teeth cannot.
A stade was a Greek measure of about 180–200 metres, so 30 stades is roughly 6 kilometres.
"Munificence" is generosity; "parsimoniousness" is stinginess. The sentence praises Greeks for spending lavishly on divine statues.
Ægis: a goat-skin shield or breastplate associated with Zeus and Athena, here a golden ornament bearing the Gorgon Medusa's head.
Tyrrhenians: the Greek name for the Etruscans of Italy.
Ante-chapel: the pronaos, the porch or vestibule in front of the temple's main chamber.
"Before the table was made": the victors' crowns were laid on this tripod until a separate table was made for them.
Stade: a Greek measure of length, roughly 180–200 metres; a building two stades long was enormous.
"Round parts of the building": apparently the rounded ends or apses of the Roman building described, where the statues stood.
Pausanias infers a Thracian origin from the founder's name, an argument from etymology.
The Eridanus was a legendary river, linked in myth with amber; Greeks often located it in the far north-west.
This second "amber" is electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver.
Wild-olive crowns were the Olympic victor's prize; Nero competed at the Games in AD 67 and dedicated crowns.
This is the treaty of 420 BC between Elis, Athens, Argos and Mantinea, made against Sparta.

context_notes.text: Campania is the region of Italy around Capua and Naples. Pausanias, a Greek traveller, is reporting something he saw in Italy.
Greek cult statues, such as Zeus at Olympia, were often made of gold and ivory. This chapter belongs to Pausanias' discussion of the ivory used at Olympia.
Antiochus is probably a Seleucid king, Antiochus IV Epiphanes, known for lavish gifts to Greek cities.
Cynisca, a Spartan princess, was the first woman to win an Olympic victory, in the four-horse chariot race.
Hadrian and Trajan were Roman emperors of the second century AD; Hadrian was a great admirer of Greece.
Trajan conquered Dacia (the Getæ's land) and campaigned against Parthia, the great eastern rival of Rome.
Nero visited Greece in AD 66–67 and competed in the Games, which were rescheduled for him.
The race in armour was a running event in which athletes carried a shield.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias asks a question that expects the answer "no one," using the earlier examples to make his claim seem obvious.
The first-person claim of eyewitness testimony reinforces Pausanias' authority as a traveller who values what he has personally seen over hearsay.
Pausanias sets the Olympian veil against the Ephesian one, using comparison to make the unfamiliar custom vivid to the reader.
A list of Trajan's buildings piles up grand structures, building an impression of imperial magnificence in a travel-guide manner.
The aside about the name shows Pausanias' habit of learned digression, interrupting description to reason like a scholar.
